headline: Kept draft home occupation zoning ordinance in committee for more work, 4-0 vote.
summary: The committee discussed a draft ordinance that would make it easier to run small businesses from homes. Members asked city staff and the City Solicitor to revise the language and resolve open questions before a joint public hearing.
decisions: Kept the draft Home Occupation Zoning Ordinance (#46 of 2025) in committee, 4-0 vote.

decision_evidence.quote: Smith motioned that this remains in committee and Hapworth seconded the motion. The motion carried 4-0.

plain_text:
City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on     Ordinances, Licenses and Legal Affairs co-posted Committee of the 
Whole______________________________________________________________________________  
met in the Council Chamber on _August 11, 2026__________ at ______7:00______P.M. 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
___ July 29, 2026__ at ___        8:20 A.M._________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
OLLA – Varela (chair), Hapworth, Smith and Holappa.  COW – Flynn, King, and Sydoriak.   From the city – Lisa Peterson, Chief of 
Staff, James Wellock, City Solicitor, David Greenbaum, Health Agent, Tom Daniel, Director of Planning & Community 
Development and Stavroula Orfanos, Building Commissioner. 
ABSENT WERE:  OLLA –Prosniewski.  COW – Davis, Merkl and Turowski.   
#46 of 2025 Draft Home Occupation Zoning Ordinance 
Varela – This is the second meeting this year on home occupation with a discussion of the draft ordinance. He explained that 
Salem’s current home-occupation rules are highly restrictive, particularly because they do not allow residents to commercially 
create products or conduct certain businesses from their homes. Other Massachusetts communities have adopted more 
flexible rules, and the goal is to determine whether Salem can similarly allow reasonable home-based activities. 
It was emphasized that the ordinance should provide clear, reasonable uses that residents can undertake by right, rather than 
forcing them through the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA). The ZBA process can be costly and burdensome and may create a 
significant barrier for economically disadvantaged residents. Uses that genuinely require additional oversight could still require 
a special permit, but ordinary and reasonable home occupations should not. 
There was a previous case involving a licensed therapist who wanted to operate a small office from her home, allowing clients 
to visit on a part-time basis. The situation became highly contentious and political, despite his view that the proposed use was 
reasonable. The example was presented as evidence that Salem needs clearer rules so that appropriate home occupations can 
be permitted without unnecessary neighborhood conflict or an onerous approval process. 
The immediate goal was to review the draft language with the city solicitor, chief of staff, and department heads, determine 
where the ordinance should go, and ultimately bring the proposal before the Planning Board. The broader objective is to give 
residents clearer guidance about what they can reasonably do in their homes while making it easier for residents to remain in 
Salem and pursue small-scale economic opportunities from home. 
Peterson - Mayor Pangallo, though unable to attend, expressed support for the proposal and appreciation for bringing it 
forward. He recognizes that people have long worked from their homes and wants the city to establish clear, reasonable 
pathways for home occupations to operate as acceptable uses.
Wellock – He supports the concept of making Salem’s home-occupation rules more flexible but expressed concerns that the 
proposed draft may be too detailed and difficult to administer and enforce. He recommended first identifying what problems 
exist with the current ordinance rather than adding numerous definitions, professions, and restrictions. He suggested a simpler 
approach to define “home occupation” broadly and make it a by-right use in appropriate zoning districts, rather than relying on 
a long, non-exhaustive list of occupations that could create ambiguity. 
Wellock also questioned several proposed restrictions and whether they address actual problems. For example, he questioned 
the practicality of enforcing a 7 p.m. cutoff, particularly for people working remotely, and suggested restrictions should be tied 
to specific concerns such as noise or traffic. He also questioned a prohibition on structural changes to a home, noting that 
someone operating a small business within the permitted portion of their property might reasonably need to expand or modify 
their space. He cautioned against creating rules that would unnecessarily put the Building Department in the position of 
denying otherwise appropriate projects. 
Overall, Wellock recommended starting with the existing ordinance, identifying the specific problems that need to be solved, 
and then making targeted, simple changes. He welcomed input from the Building Commissioner and Health Agent, who 
regularly encounter home-occupation issues, and said he looked forward to working on a revised draft. 
Green – How does the letting of rooms and lodging affect the short-term rentals since we already have a short-term rental 
ordinance?   
Daniel – He supported the goal of making Salem’s home-occupation rules clearer and easier for residents to understand and 
agreed with the City Solicitor’s recommendation to establish a clear definition of “home occupation.” He also suggested adding 
a purpose statement explaining the intent behind the ordinance, which could help future officials and residents understand 
why the rules were adopted. 
He raised several questions for the committee to consider as the draft is revised. These included why home occupations would 
require a special permit in the Business Park Development district but not elsewhere, whether the 25% space limitation should 
have an additional cap for larger accessory structures, and how the ordinance should define “immediate family” when limiting 
employees. He also questioned whether the employee rule should focus on family members or residents of the dwelling. 
Additional issues included whether to allow on-site sales, whether exterior storage should be permitted and count toward the 
space limitation, and whether exterior storage should have screening requirements. Daniel also noted questions about client 
visits, operating hours, business certificates, and how existing regulations, such as those governing commercial vehicles, should 
be incorporated or referenced without unnecessarily duplicating other city rules. 
Finally, he raised questions about signage, particularly in multifamily buildings where more than one unit has a home 
occupation. Overall, the comments were intended to identify details for further discussion and refinement rather than request 
immediate decisions on each issue. 
Discussion – 
A major discussion was about finding the right balance between allowing reasonable home-based economic activity and 
preventing neighborhood impacts. Examples discussed as potentially appropriate included professional offices, therapists, 
photographers, tutors, crafts sold online, and certain cottage-food businesses. Members generally agreed that activities such 
as automotive businesses, restaurants, or uses involving hazardous materials should not automatically qualify as home 
occupations. There was also discussion of limiting customer visits or deliveries rather than restricting the hours when a person 
could work from home. Several members expressed concern that overly broad nuisance provisions could create opportunities 
for disputes between neighbors and make enforcement subjective. 
The committee also discussed cottage-food operations and other businesses subject to separate health and safety regulations. 
The Health Agent Green explained that residential food businesses are already subject to state and local food-code 
requirements, including restrictions on what can be prepared in a residential kitchen. Members generally agreed that the 
Home Occupation Ordinance should not duplicate regulations that already exist elsewhere, but there was interest in clearly 
directing residents to the appropriate health requirements.
Another major issue was whether home occupations should be allowed entirely by right or require some form of registration 
or review. Some councilors argued that reasonable, low-impact businesses should be allowed by right, so residents do not 
have to go through a potentially costly and adversarial Zoning Board of Appeals process. Others, including the Building 
Commissioner, expressed concern that completely eliminating review could allow inappropriate or unsafe activities to operate 
without the city knowing about them. A possible compromise discussed was a simple registration or business certificate 
process, rather than a full special-permit process. This could give the city information about businesses operating in homes 
while avoiding a major barrier to entry. 
Councillors also discussed whether the ordinance should retain a list of prohibited uses rather than a lengthy list of permitted 
occupations. There was concern that a list of permitted uses would quickly become outdated as new types of businesses 
emerge. The City Solicitor favored defining the characteristics of an acceptable home occupation and potentially identifying 
certain clearly prohibited activities. The committee also discussed the possibility of creating two categories, such as minor and 
major home occupations, with low impact uses allowed by right and other uses remaining subject to special review. 
Several additional issues were identified for further drafting, including the 25% floor-area limitation, number of employees, 
operating or customer-visit hours, parking and traffic, exterior storage, on-site sales, signage, commercial vehicles, and the 
treatment of accessory structures. Members agreed that the ordinance should be simplified and should avoid duplicating 
provisions already contained elsewhere in the zoning code. 
The committee ultimately agreed that more work was needed before the ordinance could proceed to a joint public hearing. 
Members wanted city staff and the City Solicitor to work together on revised language and resolve the remaining questions 
about definitions, enforcement, registration, permitted and prohibited uses, and neighborhood protections. 
Vote 
Smith motioned that this remains in committee and Hapworth seconded the motion. The motion carried 4-0.  
On the motion of C. Smith, the meeting adjourned at 7:20 P.M. 
 
       Andrew Varela                                          mbc 
           (Chairperson)
